newsitem.title: GABON: Gabon prime minister, party win parliament seats.
newsitem.headline: Gabon prime minister, party win parliament seats.

text.p: Gabon's prime minister and a handful of members of his government were among early winners from the Central African nation's confused weekend parliamentary election, unofficial results showed on Monday.

The National Electoral Commission, which organised Sunday's poll, declined all comment on the partial results published in the government newspaper L'Union showing President Omar Bongo's Gabonese Democratic Party with 14 seats.

Father Paul Mba Abessole, head of the opposition National Woodcutters Rally which won control of the capital Libreville in chaotic local elections in October, denounced a lack of organisation and transparency.
But Abessole, questioned by Reuters on Monday, announced no immediate plans to contest Sunday's results formally.
"We took part in the elections because we did not want to adopt a boycotting policy," he said, adding his party had never trusted the government to organise the elections fairly.
The poll was part of a 1994 deal to defuse political unrest stemming from Bongo's disputed re-election a year earlier. Abessole was runner-up in that contest.
More than 1,000 candidates were bidding for 120 seats in the national assembly on Sunday. Gabon, an oil-producing ex-French colony of 1.2 million people, has an electorate of 550,000.

Citing his own case, Abessole said results showed a ruling party member had won his constituency after presidential guards and other outsiders voted there but the authorities seemed reluctant to announce that he had been beaten.
"The figures show that he won (outright) because he had over 51 percent. If they have won, let them say so," he said, adding: "They are blocked by their own figures."
Delays in distributing voting materials disrupted polling.

Abessole, who won his constituency in the local polls and is expected to become Libreville's mayor, denounced as unlawful late delivery of voter cards and late posting of electoral lists. "It's always the same, the ritual disorganisation."

Bongo, who has ruled Gabon since 1968 and the death of Gabon's founding head of state, Leon Mba, was more sanguine. "Everything has to start somewhere," he said after casting his vote on Sunday, adding that things would get better with time.

Voters in Libreville, some of whom had queued from dawn, remained calm, with no reports of major incident. Reports from elsewhere said voting stations or materials were ransacked in three southern towns with unspecified incidents in two others.
Early winners, according to L'Union, included Prime Minister Paulin Obame-Nguema, Bongo's son and advisor Ali and the ministers of oil, transport, agriculture and construction.
Past experience suggests results could take over a week to trickle out. A second round is scheduled for December 29.
Sunday's vote was Gabon's second multiparty legislative polls. The first were in 1990 when a wave of democratic reform swept across Africa after the fall of Soviet-bloc communism.
